title: Merrick and Freeport Indigenous Landscape
summary: An overview of Meroke/Merrick and Freeport-area Native history, including south shore landscape context, archaeological evidence without sensitive locations, contact-period records, public markers, and modern acknowledgment.
content:
South Shore Homeland

The Merrick and Freeport area sits within a south shore Native landscape remembered in sources through names such as Meroke, Merrick, Mericoke, Merriack, Merricock, and Mercock. Tooker connected the Merrick name with the Hempstead Plains and with meanings related to bare or open land, while colonial records place Merrick/Mericock people in a wider western Long Island network that also involved Massapequa, Rockaway, Canarsie, Secatogue, and neighboring communities. [1. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911); John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.]

This landscape is best understood as creek, meadow, bay, plain, trail, and village geography rather than as a single fixed point. Waterways and south shore meadows linked planting grounds, shellfish waters, fishing places, travel routes, and kinship relationships across the later municipal lines of Merrick, Freeport, Baldwin, Bellmore, and Hempstead. [2. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]

Archaeology And Material Culture

Local histories and archaeological readers describe shell deposits, tools, and other material traces in the broader south shore creek-and-meadow landscape, including accounts recorded in the nineteenth century and later histories of the Milburn Creek/Hick's Neck area. Those sources point to long Indigenous use of estuary resources, shellfish, wampum materials, and nearby uplands. Burial information, private findspots, and directions for artifact collecting are not included here. [3. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]

The same references also show loss. Some shell deposits were reportedly carted away for fertilizer or treated as raw material instead of protected cultural evidence. That history should be remembered as disturbance and erasure, with care taken today not to dig, collect, trespass, or disturb possible cultural material. [4. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]

Contact-Period Records

The written record begins from colonial needs, so it must be read carefully. A December 13, 1643 Hempstead deed preserves Merrick-related names and places in a land transaction involving Native representatives and English purchasers. A March 12, 1656 Dutch agreement names western Long Island allied communities in a context that included Meracock/Merrick. On July 4, 1657, Merrick village representatives were part of a Hempstead conference with leaders and interpreters including Tackapousha, Wyandanch, Cockenoe, and Mangwobe. [5. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.]

These records are not simply evidence of sale. In 1675, Tackapousha challenged Hempstead's use of Mercock land by saying it had not been paid for, making the Merrick/Freeport-area record a story of diplomacy, pressure, translation, boundary conflict, and Native legal resistance. Reverend Azariah Horton's 1742 mission journal later records preaching visits at Merrick and neighboring south shore communities, another sign that Native presence and colonial religious pressure continued into the eighteenth century. [6. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.; Long Island Historical Journal discussion of Reverend Azariah Horton's 1742 mission journal.]

Public Memory Today

A New York State historic marker placed in Merrick in the 1930s identified a Meroke village area, but that marker has been missing for many years. The missing marker is part of the modern story: public acknowledgment can appear, disappear, and need to be rebuilt through careful interpretation and local sources. [7. John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.]

Freeport is also part of the modern acknowledgment landscape. South Ocean Gallery at South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation is scheduled to host Living Conduit - Indigenous History and Present Day in fall 2026, connecting On This Site landscapes with contemporary Shinnecock portraiture and Long Island Indigenous presence. [8. SNUUC On This Site and Portrait Show pre-publicity draft; SNUUC On This Site exhibition project outline.]
why_this_matters: Merrick and Freeport are part of a Native south shore homeland and a modern public-memory landscape. The place-name, deed, mission, marker, and exhibition records all point to histories that are still present, while vulnerable cultural places remain protected.
